needs: Chapter 128 — Neurologic Diseases and Opportunistic Infections in HIV
questions.stem: A 35-year-old man was brought in by ambulance after being found unconscious. His partner gave a collateral history of preceding symptoms for 3 weeks of fevers, headaches, and new-onset seizures. He was known to have HIV but had not been on antiretroviral therapy or taking antibiotic prophylaxis. The patient was originally from Brazil but immigrated to the United States 2 years ago. On physical exam, the patient was somnolent with rightsided upper and lower extremity weakness. Investigations: CD4 count 23 cells/μL HIV viral load 76,850 copies/mL Serum Toxoplasma IgG serologies negative CSF EBV PCR negative CSF VDRL negative MRI brain: 3 discrete hypodense masses in the cerebral cortex with contrast ring enhancement
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Chagas brain abscess In patients from endemic regions, Trypanosoma cruzi can cause acute or reactivation disease, particularly in patients with advanced AIDS. The most common presentation is CNS reactivation leading to meningoencephalitis or brain abscesses, which presents very similarly to Toxoplasma with ring-enhancing lesions on MRI imaging. The negative serum Toxoplasma serologies and EBV PCR in the CSF make other causes such as toxoplasmic encephalitis or primary CNS lymphoma less likely while the patient’s country of origin in South America is endemic for Chagas disease.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q24

needs: Chapter 310 — Infections in the Immunocompromised Host
questions.stem: A 67-year-old man presented with a 2-week history of headache, nausea, vomiting, neck pain, and low-grade fever. He underwent orthotopic liver transplantation for alcoholic cirrhosis 6 months prior and was on high-dose steroids for induction and tacrolimus and mycophenolate for maintenance immunosuppression. He was on secondary prophylaxis with valganciclovir for CMV syndrome. MRI brain: multiple rim-enhancing lesions along the frontal horns of the lateral ventricles, corpus callosum, and cerebellum.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?
questions.explanation: Perform a brain biopsy The differential for this presentation is too broad, and empiricism may lead to bad outcomes. The patient underwent a stereotactic needle biopsy of the right frontal lesion. Pathology showed diffuse large B-cell lymphoma that was CD20-positive. In situ hybridization was positive for EBVencoded small RNA (EBER). A PET scan showed no activity outside of the CNS. This was a case of posttransplant primary CNS lymphoma, which carries a dismal prognosis.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q24

questions.question: A pregnant female presents at 12 weeks GA with a toxoplasma serology positive for IgM.

parts.text: What 2 non-serological tests would you perform?
What 1 treatment would you start?
If it is now at 24 weeks, what would the treatment of choice be?

cohort_answer.text: Non-serological tests: Amnio PCR at 18 weeks onwards; Fetal u/s. || Treatment: Spiramycin (maximum efficacy if given within 8 weeks of seroconversion). || At 24 weeks: Pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine + leucovorin.

parts.text: Briefly describe the IgG avidity testing in the context of a pregnant female with a positive toxoplasma IgM.
What are the implications to the fetus if it is highly avid IgG?

questions.model_answer: a) IgG avidity testing: measures the binding strength of Toxoplasma IgG antibodies to antigen; recently acquired infection produces low-avidity (weakly binding) IgG, while chronic/remote infection produces high-avidity (strongly binding) IgG that develops over months; a high-avidity result within the first trimester essentially excludes infection acquired during the current pregnancy, resolving the ambiguity of a persistently positive IgM (which can remain positive for months to years after infection). b) Implication if highly avid: high avidity indicates infection occurred more than ~3-4 months prior, i.e. before conception or very early pregnancy - this substantially lowers (essentially excludes clinically significant) risk of a new primary infection and congenital transmission to the fetus.

questions.question: 34yo woman with HIV, seizures, weakness, confusion. Intracranial lesion in gray matter with mass effect, no herniation. No CSF parameters given/ appears to be done. You suspect toxo.

parts.text: What is your treatment regimen
THIS woman is now 16 wks pregnant – how to treat?
What is the most likely alternative dx?

questions.model_answer: a) Treatment regimen for HIV/toxoplasmic encephalitis: pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine + leucovorin (folinic acid) for 6 weeks, then continue as secondary prophylaxis until CD4 >200 for ≥6 months on ART. b) At 16 weeks pregnant: pyrimethamine is relatively contraindicated in first trimester due to teratogenicity concerns; treat with pyrimethamine-sulfadiazine-leucovorin regardless in this life-threatening CNS disease (benefit outweighs risk beyond first trimester) - alternative regimens (e.g. sulfadiazine alone, or TMP-SMX) can be considered if avoiding pyrimethamine, but standard of care for maternal CNS toxoplasmosis is still pyrimethamine-sulfadiazine-leucovorin given severity. c) Most likely alternative diagnosis: primary CNS lymphoma (EBV-associated, in advanced HIV/AIDS).

questions.question: A woman who has HIV (CD4 72) presents with seizure/focal neurologic deficits. CT head demonstrates 3 large grey matter lesions, largest ~3 cm. She has not travelled anywhere and she was born in Canada – (2019)

parts.text: A) You suspect these lesions are due to toxoplasmosis - what is the first line therapy for this condition?
B) How would you treat this patient if she were 16 weeks pregnant?
C) What would your top differential diagnosis be if this ended up not being toxoplasmosis?

cohort_answer.text: First line therapy: Pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine + leucovorin for 6 weeks, followed by TMP/SMX 1 DS BID until VL suppressed and CD4 >200 for 3 months (if unable to use sulfadiazine need alternative PJP proph agent). If pregnant: HIV+ with brain lesions + pregnant = wait until 2nd trimester to use pyrimethamine, otherwise treat as per adult; discuss risks/benefits of secondary prophylaxis with TMPSMX during pregnancy; spiramycin recommended to prevent congenital transmission during primary infection in pregnancy but does not treat fetal infection; pyrimethamine/sulfadiazine/leucovorin recommended for pregnant women with strong suspicion of fetal infection, pyrimethamine avoided in first trimester due to teratogenicity. Top differential: Primary CNS lymphoma (median age 35 in HIV, often multiple lesions); other ddx: TB, PML (white matter lesions), Cryptococcal meningitis (not typical imaging), Neurocysticercosis (no travel), Bartonellosis (no exposures)

questions.question: 1 month old went to the ophthalmologist and had findings suggestive toxoplasmosis on eye exam.

parts.text: What are the three common findings in a neonate with congenital toxo that is symptomatic
Name 3 serologic tests results that would be diagnostic for congenital toxoplasmosis
Name 3 drugs that are the first line treatment of congenital toxoplasmosis

questions.model_answer: a) Three common findings in symptomatic congenital toxoplasmosis: chorioretinitis, intracranial (periventricular) calcifications, and hydrocephalus (classic triad); also microcephaly and seizures common. b) Three diagnostic serologic results for congenital toxoplasmosis: (1) Positive Toxoplasma-specific IgM or IgA in the infant (does not cross placenta, indicates fetal/neonatal production). (2) Persistently positive/rising IgG titer beyond expected decline of passively transferred maternal antibody (maternal IgG should decline and disappear by ~1 year if not truly infected). (3) Western blot showing infant-specific antibody bands not present in maternal serum (comparative immunoblotting). c) Three first-line drugs for congenital toxoplasmosis treatment: pyrimethamine, sulfadiazine, and leucovorin (folinic acid) - typically for 12 months.

questions.question: Q50 (2015). Patient has toxoplasmosis, no sulfadiazine.

parts.text: A) What are 2 other treatment options?
B) Patient has PCP, no septra. What are 2 other options for treatment?

cohort_answer.text: A) Alternative: Pyrimethamine + Clindamycin; Pyrimethamine + Atovaquone. B) Mild: Clindamycin + primaquine, Dapsone + trimethoprim, Atovaquone. Moderate: Clindamycin + primaquine, Dapsone + trimethoprim. Severe: Clindamycin + primaquine, IV pentamidine.

parts.text: Guy with vasculitis on steroids who has ring enhancing lesions in brain and lung nodules. List 3 possible organisms and first line empiric treatment regimen

cohort_answer.text: Possible organisms: Nocardia, Staph aureus, Streptococcus anginosus. Empiric treatment: Ceftriaxone, vanco, metro (empiric bacterial coverage); Septra, imipenem +/- amikacin (Nocardia); TB - RIPE + steroids if meningitis; Cryptococcus - amphoB + flucytosine, then fluconazole

questions.question: Person has a fluctuant mass in his neck with erythema, swelling and tenderness. For the following scenarios, name the most common pathogen and the most appropriate specimen and microbiologic test.

parts.text: Recently ate steak tartar
Immigrant from Vietnam, also has cough and weight loss over few weeks
Bit by a rabbit on the shoulder
Inflamed tonsils with exudate

cohort_answer.text: Steak tartar: Toxoplasma gondii. Blood serology acute and convalescent. Immigrant from Vietnam: Tuberculosis adenitis - fine needle aspiration or excisional biopsy for AFB and mycobacterial culture. Rabbit bite: Francisella tularensis, blood serology at time of presentation and 2-4 weeks after. Inflamed tonsils: Strep pyogenes. Pharyngeal culture. Parapharyngeal/retropharyngeal collection may need to be drained and can be cultured

questions.question: Toxo scenarios. Give interpretation, what do you do, and further suggestions.

parts.text: IgG NEG/IgM NEG?
IgG POS/IgM NEG?
IgG POS/IgM POS?

cohort_answer.text: IgG NEG/IgM NEG: no infection, do nothing. IgG POS/IgM NEG: remote infection with immunity. IgG POS/IgM POS: possibly acute infection but can't tell how acute, consider IgG avidity testing; look for signs of CNS infection, eye disease, or pregnancy - if present consider treatment with pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine. (In acute infection, IgM usually appears within 1 week and rises, then declines/disappears variably (sometimes over months); IgG follows within ~2 weeks, peaks ~8 weeks, generally persists for life; no direct correlation between IgG titer height and proximity of infection.)

questions.question: HIV man with CD4 <50. Had stopped Septra because of SJS. 2 weeks of fever and neurologic symptoms. CT shows multiple ring-enhancing lesions without mass effect.

parts.text: What to treat with and for how long? What secondary ppx? When do you stop?

cohort_answer.text: Toxoplasmosis gondii. HIV+ CD4<100 with space-occupying lesion involving gray matter: ddx is either toxo or lymphoma. If in endemic area: fungal, mycobacterial and parasitic also possible

questions.question: Toxoplasmosis scenario. Give interpretation, what do you do, and further investigations for: IgG-/IgM-; IgG+/IgM-; IgG+/IgM+

parts.text: Give interpretation, what do you do, and further investigations

cohort_answer.text: IgG-/IgM-: no evidence of toxo. IgG+/IgM-: probably past infection >6 months prior to pregnancy, no further testing. IgG+/IgM+: if seroconversion, may offer amniocentesis PCR and fetal US. Can send for Toxo IgG avidity testing to confirm it's a recent infection.

questions.question: Evaluation of pregnant female with ?toxo. Scenario with woman who is 6 weeks pregnant, possible exposure to toxo. Serology reveals + IgG and IgM.

parts.text: What is one test you can do to determine timing of infection?
Explain briefly how you would interpret the results of this test and why?

cohort_answer.text: A) IgG avidity testing or AC/HS pattern. The differential agglutination test ("AC/HS test") uses two antigen preparations expressing determinants found early (AC antigen) or late (HS) in infection; ratios interpreted as acute, equivocal, non-acute or non-reactive; acute pattern may persist for a year+. Best used with a panel of other tests (e.g. TSP). The IgG avidity test measures antibody binding force, low early after infection, increasing with time; high avidity indicates infection occurred at least four months earlier. B) High-avidity IgG antibodies develop at least 12-16 weeks after infection, indicating infection acquired >16 weeks earlier. In a pregnant woman early in gestation, a high-avidity IgG result indicates the fetus is essentially not at risk for congenital toxo, regardless of IgM. For pregnant women >16 weeks GA, a high-avidity test at least shows infection acquired 12-16 weeks earlier (in this scenario, the NPV of amniotic fluid PCR would be higher). Low-avidity or equivocal results can persist for a year or more and must not be used alone to determine recent infection.

questions.question: Table of toxo serology.

parts.text: Which one needs confirmatory testing?
If congenital infection at 20 weeks gestation, what do you treat her with and for how long?
What 2 other investigations are required?

cohort_answer.text: A) A positive IgM test result requires further assessment with confirmatory testing at a reference laboratory. Confirm moms with positive screening (IgM+ or equivocal) during pregnancy; screen women suspected to have acute toxoplasmosis, with risk factors, symptoms, or immunocompromised (up to 50% of women have no risk factors or are asymptomatic). B) Spiramycin is indicated for patients confirmed/suspected infected before 14 weeks gestation, continued until delivery even if amniotic fluid PCR negative/US normal. Because spiramycin does not reliably cross the placenta, if fetal infection documented/highly suspected or maternal infection acquired at 14 weeks or later, recommend sulfadiazine, pyrimethamine, and folinic acid (10-20mg daily, during and 1 week after pyrimethamine). Pyrimethamine avoided in first 14 weeks (teratogenicity); consider clindamycin instead of pyrimethamine in early pregnancy with sulfadiazine before switching to pyrimethamine. Pyrimethamine + Sulfadiazine (+leucovorin), duration until delivery for mother, for baby until age 1. C) Fetal US (look for hydrocephalus, brain or hepatic calcifications, splenomegaly, ascites); PCR of amniotic fluid at 18 weeks (sensitivity 64%, specificity 100%, NPV 88%, PPV 100%). Amniotic fluid PCR considered for women with (1) diagnostic/highly suggestive serology, (2) fetal damage on US, or (3) significant immunosuppression (except AIDS).

questions.question: Pregnant woman exposed at 19 weeks to toxoplasma. Now IgM +

parts.text: What investigations would you order and how would you manage this situation?

cohort_answer.text: If previous serology negative, repeat serology to confirm IgG conversion and proceed with amniotic fluid PCR and fetal US. Otherwise send for confirmatory serological toxo profile with IgG avidity testing.

questions.question: Q80 (2011 AM). Toxoplasma scenarios

parts.text: A. IgG NEG/IgM NEG?
B. IgG POS/IgM NEG?
C. IgG POS/IgM POS?
D. IgG NEG/IgM POS?

cohort_answer.text: A. Not toxo. B. Less likely acute toxo. C. Toxo but cannot really tell how acute infection is. D. Most likely acute toxo.

questions.question: Name two second-line treatments for the following infections

parts.text: PJP pneumonia (other than TMP-SMX)
Toxoplasmosis (other than pyrimethamine)
Stenotrophomonas (other than TMP-SMX)

cohort_answer.text:
PJP pneumonia: Mild to moderate: Atovaquone; Clindamycin-Primaquine; Dapsone/TMP. Severe disease: Clindamycin-Primaquine (check for G6PD); IV Pentamidine (toxic). Prophylaxis: Dapsone; Atovoquone; Aerosolized pentamidine
Toxoplasmosis: Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole monotherapy; Atovoquone alone; Atovoquone + sulfadiazine
Stenotrophomonas: Levofloxacin, moxi; Minocycline; Tigecycline; Ceftazidime (resistance is high); Colistin. Mechanism of resistance: multidrug-resistant efflux pumps, β-lactamases, and aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes, reduced permeability of the outer membrane

questions.question: 18. Drug shortage in a hospital

parts.text: How would you treat the following conditions if the listed drug were not available? (3) Infection / Cannot Use / Treatment Options for: PJP, Toxoplasma, Stenotrophomonas

questions.model_answer: If preferred agent unavailable: PJP - TMP-SMX unavailable: use IV pentamidine (severe disease) or clindamycin plus primaquine (mild-moderate disease); atovaquone for mild disease/prophylaxis. Toxoplasma - preferred pyrimethamine/sulfadiazine/leucovorin unavailable: use TMP-SMX, or clindamycin plus pyrimethamine/leucovorin, or atovaquone-based regimen. Stenotrophomonas - TMP-SMX unavailable: use levofloxacin, or ceftazidime/minocycline, or combination of ticarcillin-clavulanate depending on susceptibility.
questions.beyond_mandell: Based on established alternative-agent guidance for PJP, toxoplasmosis, and Stenotrophomonas maltophilia when TMP-SMX unavailable

questions.question: 50yo M HIV positive patient with CD4 count 50copies/mL, non-compliant with ART presenting with ataxia and vague neuro symptoms, no headaches. No focal neuro symptoms on exam. No history of travel, lives in Toronto. No LP given. MRI brain shows diffuse multifocal lesions.

parts.text: Give 4 pathogens and their associated syndromes to explain the clinical presentation.

questions.model_answer: Four pathogens and associated syndromes explaining diffuse multifocal brain lesions with ataxia in advanced untreated HIV (CD4 <50): (1) JC virus - progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML), causing multifocal, non-enhancing white matter lesions with subacute focal deficits, ataxia, and cognitive decline. (2) Toxoplasma gondii - toxoplasmic encephalitis, typically multiple ring-enhancing lesions with mass effect, though can present with ataxia/ill-defined symptoms if cerebellar involvement. (3) Cytomegalovirus - CMV encephalitis/ventriculoencephalitis, diffuse periventricular lesions, altered mental status, can cause ataxia and cranial nerve findings. (4) Primary CNS lymphoma (EBV-associated) - single or multiple enhancing mass lesions, can present with diffuse neurologic symptoms and ataxia depending on location.

questions.question: 14. Second Line Drug Options (Name 2 for each): a) PJP Pneumonia; b) CNS Toxoplasma (if can't use pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine + leucovorin); c) Stenotrophomonas pneumonia (if TMP-SMX contraindicated)

parts.text: a) PJP Pneumonia - second line options
b) CNS Toxoplasma - second line options
c) Stenotrophomonas pneumonia - second line options

cohort_answer.text:
Primaquine + Clindamycin (favoured); IV Pentamidine (mild: Dapsone + Trimethoprim)
Pyrimethamine + Clindamycin + folinic acid; TMP-SMX
Levofloxacin; Minocycline; Polymyxin; Cefiderocol; Ceftazidime

questions.question: Drug shortage in a hospital.

parts.text: How would you treat PJP, Toxoplasma, and Stenotrophomonas infections if Septra, Sulfadiazine, and Ticarcillin/Clav or Septra respectively were not available? (give two treatment options each)
A patient with enterococcus infective endocarditis has high level aminoglycoside resistance. What is one issue with using streptomycin?

cohort_answer.text: PJP (no Septra): Severe: Pentamidine 4mg/kg IV, or Clindamycin 450mg PO q6h + Primaquine 15-30mg PO q24h x21d; Mild-moderate: Atovaquone 750mg PO BID with food x21d. Toxoplasma (no Sulfadiazine): Clindamycin 300mg PO q8h + Pyrimethamine, or Atovaquone 750mg PO BID + pyrimethamine. Stenotrophomonas (no Ticarcillin/Clav or Septra): Minocycline 200mg IV x1 then 100mg IV BID, or Levofloxacin 750mg IV/PO q24h, ceftazidime, colistin, cefiderocol. Streptomycin issue: high level resistance = growth in presence of high concentration of streptomycin or gentamicin, meaning no synergistic AG effect possible in vivo if resistant to both; cannot extrapolate resistance of one aminoglycoside based on the other

questions.question: 18. A woman who has HIV (CD4 72) presents with seizure/focal neurologic deficits. CT head demonstrates 3 large grey matter lesions, largest ~3 cm. You suspect this is due to toxoplasmosis.

parts.text: 1st Line Regimen
Regimen if 16 weeks pregnant
Most likely alternative diagnosis

cohort_answer.text: 1st line: Pyrimethamine 200mg x1 dose then 75mg/day PO + Sulfadiazine 1.5g PO q6h + Folinic acid 25mg/day; alternative Septra 10mg/kg/day (TMP component) IV/PO divided q12h. If <60kg, Sulfadiazine dose 1g QID. Pregnant (16 weeks): Pyrimethamine 200mg x1 then 75mg/day PO + Sulfadiazine 1.5g PO q6h + Folinic acid 25mg/day; alternative Pyrimethamine + Clindamycin + Leucovorin. Alternative diagnosis: CNS lymphoma; also MTB, Cryptococcus.

questions.question: Gentleman with HIV has lived in Toronto his entire life. Noncompliant with ART and CD4 is 50. Presents with 3 weeks of altered LOC and ataxia. MRI shows scattered white matter lesions without mass effect.

parts.text: What are the 4 most likely organisms and diseases they cause?

cohort_answer.text: PML - JC Virus; CMV; HSV; VZV; TB (possible to get hydrocephalus though). Other differentials more likely to have mass effect/increased ICP: Toxoplasmosis, Cryptococcal. Non-infectious ddx: CNS lymphoma (causes mass effect).

questions.question: How would you treat the following conditions if the listed drugs were not available? Infection | Cannot Use | Treatment Options: PJP | Septra; Toxoplasma | Sulfadiazine; Stenotrophomonas | Ticarcillin-clavulanic acid or Septra

parts.text: Fill in treatment options for each infection
b) A patient with enterococcus infective endocarditis has high level aminoglycoside resistance. What is one issue with using streptomycin? (0.5)

cohort_answer.text: PJP: 1. Clindamycin-primaquine 2. Atovaquone (mild) or TMP-dapsone (mild) 3. IV pentamidine (severe). Toxoplasma: 1. Pyrimethamine-atovaquone 2. Pyrimethamine-clindamycin 3. Septra or atovaquone. Stenotrophomonas: 1. 2 of: Cefiderocol, minocycline, levofloxacin 2. Ceftazidime-avibactam AND aztreonam. b) Need access to lab for rapid streptomycin level testing; need CrCl >50; lack of familiarity amongst clinicians for streptomycin use; drug availability; high rate of ototoxicity which may not be reversible.

questions.question: A 32-year-old woman, who has never left Canada, presents to ED with fevers, confusion, and headache. She is found to have a CD4 count of 72 cells/mm3 and an MRI that shows 2-3 grey matter lesions. A clinical diagnosis of toxoplasmosis is made.

parts.text: What is the first line treatment for toxoplasmosis?
If this woman was 16 weeks pregnant, what would the first line treatment be?
What is the MOST likely alternative diagnosis, if not toxoplasmosis?

questions.model_answer: a) First-line treatment for toxoplasmic encephalitis: pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine + leucovorin (folinic acid) for 6 weeks. b) At 16 weeks pregnant: pyrimethamine avoided if possible in first trimester due to teratogenicity, but for CNS disease (life-threatening) treatment should not be withheld - use pyrimethamine-sulfadiazine-leucovorin beyond first trimester (16 weeks is second trimester, so standard regimen is appropriate); leucovorin mitigates pyrimethamine-related bone marrow suppression. c) Most likely alternative diagnosis: primary CNS lymphoma.

questions.question: Q34. 26M from Nigeria, presents with generalized seizure. No illness or fever preceding. CT shows a ring-enhancing lesion in the R temporal lobe.

parts.text: A) What are your 2 top diagnoses?

cohort_answer.text: Neurocysticercosis, Tuberculoma, Bacterial abscess, Toxoplasmosis (more in HIV pts; classic CT appearance in 90% of patients is rounded isodense or hypodense lesions with ring enhancement after contrast, multiple in 70-80%, usually at corticomedullary junction and basal ganglia), CNS lymphoma, Cryptococcoma.

questions.question: 15 year old with HIV, poorly controlled off ARVs. Comes in with focal neurological signs and seizures, ring enhancing lesions. Had SJS to septra previously. Not on ppx.

parts.text: A) Most likely diagnosis
B) Treatment, when to stop secondary ppx

cohort_answer.text:
CNS toxoplasmosis
Pyrimethamine + Clindamycin (+leucovorin/folinic acid) x6 weeks then secondary suppression. Stop secondary ppx once CD4 >200 on ARVs for >3 months, no further signs/sx of toxo encephalopathy. Secondary ppx for septra allergy: Atovaquone

questions.question: Drug shortage in a hospital.

parts.text: How would you treat PJP, Toxoplasma, and Stenotrophomonas if Septra, Sulfadiazine, and Ticarcillin-clavulanic acid/Septra respectively were not available (2 options each)?

cohort_answer.text: PJP (cannot use Septra): Pentamidine; Atovaquone. Toxoplasma (cannot use Sulfadiazine): Pyrimethamine + clindamycin + leucovorin; Atovaquone + septra + leucovorin; Atovaquone +/- pyrimethamine + Septra + leucovorin. Stenotrophomonas (cannot use Ticarcillin-clavulanic acid or Septra): Tigecycline (black box for death); Levofloxacin; Minocycline
